description: V2 recommendation library keyed to DOC-151 question IDs. Stub entries generated from assessment questions; refine per DOC-153.

templates.title: Centralize workforce identity and authentication
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate user authentication is not fully managed through a centralized identity platform. This finding reflects self-reported assessment information, not an independent technical audit of every system.

Recommended action: Inventory business applications that authenticate users separately. Select or strengthen a primary identity provider for workforce sign-in. Federate or consolidate high-value applications where practical, and define an ownership model for identity administration. Ensure leavers and role changes are processed from the same source of truth.

Expected outcome: Identity administration becomes more consistent, access changes are easier to execute correctly, and security controls such as MFA and password policy can be applied more uniformly.

Implementation considerations: Plan application-by-application cutover to avoid locking users out of line-of-business systems. Confirm licensing, directory sync, and break-glass admin accounts before enforcing centralized sign-in. Coordinate with any existing MSP or internal IT so current support processes remain workable.
templates.businessImpact: Without a central identity platform, account provisioning, access removal, and password policy become inconsistent across systems. That increases the chance of leftover access after role changes or departures, raises help-desk overhead, and makes it harder to contain unauthorized access if credentials are misused.

templates.title: Require multi-factor authentication for privileged and business-critical access
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate multi-factor authentication (MFA) is not consistently required for privileged accounts and business-critical systems. This is based on assessment answers, not a verified penetration test.

Recommended action: Identify privileged roles and systems that handle finance, email, remote access, cloud admin, and customer data. Enforce MFA for those accounts first, then expand to remaining workforce access as capacity allows. Prefer phishing-resistant methods where practical for administrators. Document exception handling and recovery procedures for lost authenticators.

Expected outcome: Credential theft alone becomes less likely to grant immediate access to high-impact systems, reducing the probability and blast radius of account-takeover incidents.

Implementation considerations: Start with privileged and remote-access paths to limit business disruption. Communicate rollout timing, enroll backup factors, and retain a controlled break-glass process. Align MFA policy with the identity platform already in use wherever possible.
templates.businessImpact: Password-only access to admin accounts and critical systems is a common path to ransomware, fraud, and data theft. For an SMB, a single compromised privileged credential can interrupt operations, expose customer or financial data, and create costly recovery work.

templates.title: Replace shared employee credentials with individual accounts
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate employees may still rely on shared credentials rather than individual accounts for some systems. This reflects reported practices, not a completed credential audit of every application.

Recommended action: Inventory systems that use shared usernames or passwords. Create individual accounts with appropriate roles, migrate users, retire shared credentials, and store any unavoidable service accounts in a controlled secret store with limited ownership. Update onboarding and offboarding checklists accordingly.

Expected outcome: Access activity can be attributed to a person, offboarding becomes more reliable, and the organization reduces the risk that one shared password unlocks broad business access.

Implementation considerations: Some legacy applications only support a single login—document those exceptions, compensate with monitoring or network controls where needed, and schedule replacement or upgrade when practical. Coordinate password changes carefully to avoid downtime.
templates.businessImpact: Shared logins remove personal accountability, complicate offboarding, and make it difficult to investigate misuse. When several people share one password, a single disclosure can expose multiple business functions and extend unauthorized access after someone leaves.

templates.title: Separate privileged administrator accounts from everyday user accounts
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate administrators may not use separate privileged accounts for elevated tasks. This is assessment-reported and should be confirmed during remediation discovery.

Recommended action: Issue dedicated privileged accounts for administration of servers, cloud tenants, firewalls, and identity systems. Require MFA on those accounts, prohibit their use for day-to-day email and browsing, and limit standing privileges where just-in-time elevation is available. Review who holds privileged roles quarterly.

Expected outcome: Everyday account compromise is less likely to yield immediate administrative control, improving containment options and reducing privileged misuse risk.

Implementation considerations: Establish clear naming, vaulting, and break-glass procedures before disabling shared admin habits. Train administrators on when to elevate. Avoid creating unmanaged local admin sprawl as a substitute.
templates.businessImpact: When administrators use the same account for email and privileged work, routine phishing or malware on a daily workstation can escalate to full system control. That elevates operational disruption risk and increases the cost of containment after an incident.

templates.title: Document and operate a joiner–mover–leaver access process
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate a documented joiner, mover, and leaver process is incomplete or missing. Findings are based on assessment responses rather than an HR or directory audit.

Recommended action: Define standard steps for hire, role change, and termination covering account creation, approvals, group membership, MFA enrollment, and timely disablement. Assign owners between HR/operations and IT, use checklists or tickets as the system of record, and measure time-to-revoke for leavers.

Expected outcome: Access more closely matches current job needs, departed users are disabled promptly, and audits or investigations have a clearer trail of who approved what.

Implementation considerations: Keep the process lightweight for SMB scale—simple checklists often outperform unused complex workflows. Integrate with the identity platform and ticketing tools already in place. Pilot with one department before company-wide enforcement.
templates.businessImpact: Without a defined lifecycle process, new hires may receive inconsistent access, role changes leave excess permissions in place, and departed users retain accounts. That creates avoidable security exposure and recurring administrative cleanup for owners and IT providers.

templates.title: Apply least-privilege access aligned to job roles
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate users may not be limited to the access required for their jobs. This is a self-reported maturity indicator, not proof of a specific data exposure.

Recommended action: Define role-based access baselines for common job functions. Review high-risk applications (finance, email admin, file shares, line-of-business systems) and remove unnecessary rights. Prefer group-based assignment over one-off exceptions, and require approval for elevated access.

Expected outcome: Fewer people can reach sensitive systems by default, which reduces blast radius and clarifies ownership of exceptions.

Implementation considerations: Expect negotiation with department leads about "convenience" access. Phase reviews by application criticality. Preserve emergency access paths that are monitored and time-bounded rather than permanent broad rights.
templates.businessImpact: Broad or inherited permissions increase the damage from mistakes, insider misuse, or stolen credentials. Excess access also creates compliance and customer-trust concerns when staff can reach data unrelated to their role.

templates.title: Enforce modern password and authentication policies centrally
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate password requirements may not be centrally enforced using modern practices. This reflects assessment answers, not a password-strength audit of all accounts.

Recommended action: Standardize policy in the primary identity provider: suitable length, protection against known breached passwords where available, sensible lockout/throttling, and MFA as the primary control rather than frequent forced rotation alone. Align federated apps to inherit these controls and retire conflicting local policies where possible.

Expected outcome: Authentication strength becomes more consistent across systems, reducing weak-password exposure and simplifying support.

Implementation considerations: Communicate changes to staff before enforcement. Avoid abrupt lockouts on shared or service accounts—inventory them first. Coordinate with applications that cannot inherit IdP policy so compensating controls are documented.
templates.businessImpact: Weak or inconsistent password rules across systems increase the likelihood of credential stuffing and reuse attacks. Fragmented policy also raises help-desk load and creates uneven protection between critical and secondary applications.

templates.title: Secure remote access with strong authentication and encryption
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate remote access may not be consistently secured with strong authentication and encryption. This is assessment-reported and should be validated against current VPN, RDP, and cloud remote-access configurations during remediation.

Recommended action: Inventory remote access methods (VPN, RDP gateways, cloud admin portals, vendor connections). Require MFA, disable unused exposure, enforce encrypted transport, restrict source networks where practical, and replace legacy direct RDP-to-Internet patterns with hardened gateways or modern remote-access controls.

Expected outcome: Remote work and vendor support continue with a lower likelihood that Internet-facing access alone yields easy account or session takeover.

Implementation considerations: Schedule changes during maintenance windows. Maintain out-of-band recovery access for administrators. Coordinate with any third-party support providers who rely on remote entry so their access is intentional and logged.
templates.businessImpact: Exposed or weakly protected remote access is a frequent entry point for ransomware and unauthorized data access. For distributed or hybrid teams, insecure remote paths can interrupt operations and create significant recovery costs.

templates.title: Review user permissions on a recurring schedule
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate user permissions are not reviewed periodically in a reliable way. This finding is based on reported process maturity, not a completed entitlement scan.

Recommended action: Establish a lightweight quarterly (or semiannual) access review for critical systems and privileged groups. Provide managers with simple membership lists, capture attestations, and remove access that is no longer needed. Track overdue reviews.

Expected outcome: Excess access is pruned regularly, improving accountability and reducing long-lived unnecessary privileges.

Implementation considerations: Focus first on privileged roles, finance systems, and shared mailboxes/files. Keep reviews short enough that managers complete them. Automate exports from the identity platform where possible.
templates.businessImpact: Permissions accumulate over time as people change roles. Without periodic review, dormant access increases unauthorized-use risk and makes investigations slower when something goes wrong.

templates.title: Assign clear ownership for identity and access management
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate responsibility for identity and access management may not be clearly assigned. This is an organizational finding from the assessment, not a technical vulnerability claim.

Recommended action: Name a primary owner (and backup) for identity platform administration, access approvals, and joiner–mover–leaver execution. Document decision rights versus the IT provider or MSP. Include identity topics in a recurring operations review.

Expected outcome: Ownership clarity improves response time for access changes and gives leadership a single point of accountability for identity risk.

Implementation considerations: Ownership can sit with an internal manager supported by an external provider; the key is documented responsibility. Avoid distributing admin rights widely as a substitute for ownership.
templates.businessImpact: When nobody owns identity administration, provisioning and revocation become ad hoc. Gaps show up during employee changes, audits, and incidents—creating avoidable downtime and unclear accountability between leadership and IT support.

templates.title: Maintain an accurate company-owned device inventory
templates.description:
Finding: An accurate inventory of company-owned devices is missing or incomplete based on the assessment response. “No” typically means no reliable device list; “Partially” usually means lists exist but omit sites, remote workers, or recently issued hardware.

Recommended action: Build a living inventory of company-owned endpoints in scope (workstations, laptops, tablets, and other managed portable devices). Capture identifier, assigned user or role, site or remote status, OS, and warranty or purchase date where known. Reconcile against procurement, directory, and support tooling on a defined cadence and after hire, transfer, or offboarding events.

Expected outcome: Security and support coverage decisions are based on what the organization actually owns, reducing blind spots in patching, encryption, and retirement.

Implementation considerations: Focus first on devices that access business email, line-of-business apps, or customer data. Reuse existing management or directory sources where available rather than maintaining a disconnected spreadsheet. Distinguish company-owned from BYOD if personal devices are in use. Complements broader technology inventory work (Documentation & Knowledge) by staying endpoint-specific.
templates.businessImpact: When company-owned workstations, laptops, and related devices are not inventoried accurately, patching, encryption, support, and retirement work miss systems. Lost or forgotten devices also raise data-exposure risk after departure or theft.

templates.title: Document and run a device lifecycle process
templates.description:
Finding: A documented device lifecycle is missing or only partially defined. “No” suggests procurement, deployment, refresh, and retirement are ad hoc; “Partially” suggests some steps exist without end-to-end ownership or consistent execution.

Recommended action: Document the endpoint lifecycle from request and procurement through imaging, assignment, refresh, redeployment, and secure retirement. Define target ages or warranty triggers for replacement classes, and a checklist for wiping, reclaiming licenses, and removing accounts when devices leave service. Publish the process to IT support and business requestors.

Expected outcome: Device spend and risk become more predictable, and retired hardware is less likely to retain business data or active access.

Implementation considerations: Align refresh windows with budget planning. Keep the document practical—flowcharts and checklists beat unused policy prose. Coordinate with hardware lifecycle planning in Technology Strategy so endpoint practice and capital planning do not diverge.
templates.businessImpact: Without a clear device lifecycle, organizations overpay for aging hardware, rush emergency replacements, and leave retired devices with residual data or accounts. Lifecycle gaps also make warranty, imaging, and redeployment inconsistent.

templates.title: Patch operating systems and applications consistently
templates.description:
Finding: Operating systems and applications are not patched consistently across endpoints. “No” typically means patching is reactive or absent; “Partially” usually means some devices or products are updated while others lag, including remote or infrequently connected machines.

Recommended action: Define patch expectations by device class and product set (OS plus common business applications). Use centralized update or management tooling where available, report compliance, and remediate chronic exceptions. Include a path for emergency updates when actively exploited issues affect in-scope software.

Expected outcome: Exposure windows shrink for known endpoint vulnerabilities, and update practice becomes measurable rather than dependent on individual user habits.

Implementation considerations: Balance speed with change risk for specialty apps. Plan maintenance windows for shared or production-adjacent workstations. Complements Security Operations vulnerability assessment and critical-system update recommendations by focusing on endpoint OS/application consistency rather than full environment scanning.
templates.businessImpact: Inconsistent endpoint patching leaves known defects available longer and creates uneven risk across users. Unpatched browsers, office suites, and operating systems are frequent entry paths for malware and account compromise in SMB environments.

templates.title: Protect endpoints with centrally managed security software
templates.description:
Finding: Endpoints are not fully covered by centrally managed security software. “No” suggests protection is missing or unmanaged; “Partially” suggests some devices have agents while others—often remotes, specialty machines, or newly issued hardware—do not report to a central console.

Recommended action: Deploy or complete rollout of centrally managed endpoint protection for in-scope company devices. Confirm agents report health and detections to a monitored console, define who triages alerts, and remediate offline or unprotected devices. Cover common Windows and, where used, macOS business fleets in scope.

Expected outcome: Malware and suspicious endpoint activity are more likely to be detected and contained with consistent policy, rather than relying on unmonitored local tools.

Implementation considerations: Validate licensing and OS compatibility before forced rollout. Exclude only intentional exceptions with owners and review dates. Align alert routing with existing security monitoring ownership so detections are not orphaned.
templates.businessImpact: Endpoints without centrally managed security software are harder to protect consistently and harder to investigate when something goes wrong. Local-only or missing protection increases the chance that malware or unauthorized tools persist unnoticed.

templates.title: Encrypt portable devices that store or cache business data
templates.description:
Finding: Encryption is missing or incomplete on portable devices that store or cache business data. “No” typically means full-disk or equivalent encryption is not required for those devices; “Partially” usually means some portable devices are encrypted while others—or recovery key escrow—are inconsistent.

Recommended action: Require encryption on company-owned portable devices that store or cache business data (for example laptops and tablets used for email, files, or line-of-business apps). Prefer platform-native full-disk encryption managed centrally where practical, verify compliance, and escrow recovery keys with authorized administrators. Remediate exceptions before those devices travel or leave the premises routinely.

Expected outcome: Lost or stolen portable hardware that held business data is far less likely to expose readable content.

Implementation considerations: Confirm performance and compatibility on older hardware. Document recovery-key access for support without sharing keys broadly. Clarify BYOD expectations separately if personal devices access company data. Stationary desktops without portable data risk are out of scope unless they similarly store unprotected business data that travels with removable media.
templates.businessImpact: Unencrypted portable devices that store or cache business data turn loss or theft into a likely data-exposure event. Encryption reduces the chance that those files remain readable if hardware leaves organizational control.

templates.title: Enable remote management for company devices
templates.description:
Finding: Devices cannot be reliably managed remotely, or remote management covers only part of the fleet. “No” suggests no remote tooling; “Partially” suggests coverage gaps for remotes, specialty roles, or devices that never check in.

Recommended action: Place in-scope company endpoints under a remote management capability that supports inventory, scripted or policy-based maintenance, and guided support. Ensure devices check in regularly, including remote workers, and define how offline devices are brought back into management. Use remote actions only through authorized support roles.

Expected outcome: Support and security maintenance can proceed without waiting for devices to return on-site, improving response time for common issues and urgent updates.

Implementation considerations: Respect privacy and change-control expectations—document what remote actions are allowed. Confirm network and identity prerequisites for agent installation. Pair with ownership so unmanaged devices are escalated rather than ignored.
templates.businessImpact: Without remote management, routine support, patching, and emergency response depend on physical access or user-driven steps. That slows incident response and increases downtime when staff work remotely or across sites.

templates.title: Standardize endpoint configurations
templates.description:
Finding: Standard device configurations are not used consistently. “No” typically means each device is built uniquely; “Partially” usually means a baseline exists but is frequently bypassed or not applied to remotes and specialty roles.

Recommended action: Define a small set of approved endpoint baselines (for example, standard workstation and remote laptop) covering OS build, core applications, security agents, and local policy. Image or provision new devices from those baselines, and remediate drift on existing devices where practical. Document justified exceptions with owners.

Expected outcome: New devices are ready faster, support is more predictable, and security settings are applied uniformly rather than negotiated per machine.

Implementation considerations: Keep baseline count small. Involve application owners for specialty software so the standard is usable. Revisit baselines when major OS versions change.
templates.businessImpact: One-off device builds create support variation, weaken security baselines, and make onboarding slower. Standard configurations reduce “works on my machine” failures and make policy enforcement practical.

templates.title: Monitor endpoint hardware health
templates.description:
Finding: Hardware health monitoring for endpoints is missing or limited. “No” suggests failures are discovered only when users report them; “Partially” suggests some alerts exist without consistent coverage or follow-up.

Recommended action: Enable health signals available through existing management tooling (disk failure warnings, critical hardware alerts) for in-scope endpoints. Define who reviews alerts and how failing devices are scheduled for repair or replacement before total failure when possible.

Expected outcome: Failing hardware is caught earlier, reducing abrupt outages and last-minute device swaps that interrupt business work.

Implementation considerations: Start with high-impact warning types to avoid alert noise. Not every consumer laptop exposes rich telemetry—focus on actionable signals. Coordinate replacements with lifecycle and warranty records.
templates.businessImpact: Undetected disk, battery, or hardware faults lead to surprise downtime and data-loss risk when devices fail mid-work. Light health monitoring shifts replacements from emergency to planned work.

templates.title: Keep endpoint operating systems on vendor-supported versions
templates.description:
Finding: Endpoint operating systems are not consistently vendor supported. “No” typically means unsupported versions remain in production use; “Partially” usually means most devices are current while a material subset remains on end-of-support releases.

Recommended action: Inventory OS versions across company endpoints, identify unsupported or soon-to-be-unsupported releases, and schedule upgrades or hardware replacement for those devices. Prioritize machines that access email, finance, or customer systems. Track exceptions with owners and target exit dates.

Expected outcome: Endpoints remain eligible for security updates and modern management controls, reducing concentrated risk on aging OS versions.

Implementation considerations: Some specialty apps pin OS versions—plan application testing before forced upgrades. Budget may require phased waves. Do not equate “still boots” with “still supportable.”
templates.businessImpact: Unsupported operating systems stop receiving security updates and compatible tooling, concentrating risk on the users still running them. That also blocks modern endpoint protection and identity controls that assume a supported OS.

templates.title: Assign ownership for endpoint management
templates.description:
Finding: Endpoint management ownership is missing or unclear. “No” suggests no accountable owner; “Partially” suggests informal responsibility without authority, cadence, or coverage of the full fleet.

Recommended action: Assign a primary owner (internal or provider lead) accountable for endpoint inventory accuracy, protection coverage, patch posture, and lifecycle execution. Define a simple review cadence and escalation path when devices fall out of compliance. Communicate the owner to support staff and business leaders who request devices.

Expected outcome: Endpoint work has a durable owner, so gaps are remediated and rechecked rather than rediscovered each assessment cycle.

Implementation considerations: Ownership can sit with an MSP account lead plus an internal business sponsor. Authority to set standards matters more than deep technical skill. Align with broader technology leadership so endpoint decisions are not orphaned.
templates.businessImpact: Without a named owner, inventory, patching, encryption, and lifecycle work stall between IT providers and business leaders. Ambiguous ownership is a common reason endpoint gaps recur after one-time cleanup projects.

templates.title: Use networking equipment that meets business reliability and support needs
templates.description:
Finding: Networking equipment on critical business paths may not meet reliability, manageability, or supportability needs based on the assessment response. “No” typically means key paths rely on gear that is difficult to manage or support; “Partially” usually means some sites or segments meet business requirements while others do not. Suitability depends on role and risk—not every consumer-labeled device is automatically unsuitable in every scenario.

Recommended action: Identify networking devices that carry business traffic (internet edge, core switching, wireless serving offices, and site-to-site links). For each critical path, confirm the equipment can be managed, monitored, and supported to the organization’s requirements (configuration access, logging, warranty or vendor support, and replacement practicality). Upgrade or isolate devices that cannot meet those needs; leave appropriately sized solutions in place where they already satisfy business requirements. Record make/model, support contacts, and warranty or subscription status for the in-scope fleet.

Expected outcome: Critical connectivity paths are more reliable and supportable, with clearer options for configuration, monitoring, and replacement when devices fail.

Implementation considerations: Prioritize the internet edge and shared office infrastructure before specialty closets. Match equipment class to business requirements rather than brand labels alone. Reuse existing cabling and rack space where practical. Coordinate cutovers outside peak business hours. Complements Technology Strategy hardware lifecycle planning without duplicating endpoint device refresh work.
templates.businessImpact: Networking equipment that cannot be reliably managed, monitored, or supported increases outage risk on paths the business depends on. Gaps in manageability and supportability also make security changes and replacements slower when failures occur.

templates.title: Protect the network with a properly configured firewall
templates.description:
Finding: Firewall protection is missing, unmanaged, or incompletely configured. “No” typically means no business firewall is in place or rules are effectively open; “Partially” usually means a firewall exists but defaults, unused rules, or unmanaged changes leave material gaps.

Recommended action: Place a managed firewall at the primary internet edge (and secondary edges where separate circuits exist). Define allow rules based on business need, remove unused or overly broad permits, enable logging for security-relevant events, and assign who reviews rule changes. Confirm remote-access and published services are intentional rather than accidental.

Expected outcome: Inbound and outbound traffic follow known business needs, reducing exposure from open ports and unmanaged edge devices.

Implementation considerations: Schedule rule reviews after major application or VPN changes. Coordinate with Security Operations monitoring so firewall logs are watched. Avoid vendor lock-in language—focus on configuration ownership and change control. Do not equate “firewall appliance present” with “rules are appropriate.”
templates.businessImpact: Without a properly configured firewall at the network edge, unauthorized inbound access and poorly controlled outbound paths increase breach and ransomware risk. Misconfigured or unused firewalls create a false sense of protection while leaving business systems exposed.

templates.title: Make wireless connectivity reliable and secure
templates.description:
Finding: Wireless is not reliably secure or performant across business locations. “No” typically means coverage, capacity, or security basics are absent; “Partially” usually means some areas work well while guest networks, shared credentials, or weak encryption remain.

Recommended action: Assess coverage for primary work areas and meeting spaces, separate guest from business SSIDs, and require modern encryption with unique or directory-backed access rather than a single shared password for staff networks. Remediate dead zones and interference that block business work. Document SSID purpose and who may join each network.

Expected outcome: Staff can connect productively while guest and unknown devices stay off business segments, reducing both downtime friction and wireless-borne risk.

Implementation considerations: Survey before buying denser hardware. Align guest access with acceptable-use expectations. Coordinate with network segmentation so wireless gains are not undermined by flat LAN design (NW-004).
templates.businessImpact: Unreliable or weakly secured wireless slows staff, invites guest/device sprawl onto business networks, and creates a common path for unauthorized access. Dead zones and shared passwords also drive shadow hotspots that bypass intended controls.

templates.title: Segment the network to limit unnecessary access
templates.description:
Finding: Network segmentation is missing or incomplete. “No” typically means a flat LAN where most devices share broad reachability; “Partially” usually means some VLANs or zones exist without consistent enforcement for guests, IoT, servers, or remote-access entry points.

Recommended action: Define practical zones for at least business workstations, servers/line-of-business systems, guests, and any IoT or specialty devices in scope. Enforce separation with firewall or switch controls so zones only exchange traffic required for business functions. Document allowed paths and revisit when new systems are added.

Expected outcome: Compromise or misbehavior in one zone is less likely to reach critical systems immediately, improving containment and support clarity.

Implementation considerations: Start with high-value separations (guest vs business, workstations vs servers/backups) rather than an elaborate microsegmentation program. Test print, VoIP, and application paths after changes. Align with firewall rule hygiene (NW-002) and remote-access design (NW-005).
templates.businessImpact: Flat networks let a single compromised device or guest reach servers, backups, and line-of-business systems. Appropriate segmentation contains incidents and reduces accidental access to sensitive systems.

templates.title: Secure remote connectivity for offsite access
templates.description:
Finding: Remote connectivity is not securely designed or consistently applied. “No” typically means ad hoc remote access without a managed standard; “Partially” usually means some staff use secure methods while others rely on exposed services or shared access paths.

Recommended action: Standardize on a managed remote-access approach (for example VPN or equivalent brokered access) with unique user authentication and MFA where the identity platform supports it. Disable unused direct remote-desktop exposure to the internet. Define who may grant remote access and how access is removed at offboarding.

Expected outcome: Offsite work uses a known, controlled path, reducing exposure from open remote services and shared remote credentials.

Implementation considerations: Coordinate with Identity & Access for MFA and joiner/mover/leaver processes—this recommendation focuses on the network remote-access path, not full identity redesign. Test performance for common business apps. Document break-glass access for IT support.
templates.businessImpact: Insecure remote access (shared credentials, exposed remote desktop, or unmanaged tunnels) is a frequent entry point for account takeover and ransomware. Weak remote design also makes support and offboarding unreliable.

templates.title: Establish an internet resilience strategy for business continuity
templates.description:
Finding: An appropriate internet resilience strategy is missing or incomplete. “No” typically means a single circuit with no failover plan; “Partially” usually means a backup path exists but is untested, undersized, or unknown to staff who would use it.

Recommended action: Document primary and backup internet options (secondary circuit, LTE/5G failover, or temporary hotspot policy for critical roles). Define what must stay online first (payments, email/collaboration, phone, line-of-business apps). Test failover at a defined cadence and record who declares and communicates an outage.

Expected outcome: Internet disruptions become manageable degradations with a known temporary path, rather than complete business freezes.

Implementation considerations: Match investment to downtime tolerance—resilience can be a tested process before a second dedicated circuit. Align with Data Protection business continuity planning for non-network workarounds. Avoid overpromising carrier SLAs the organization does not purchase.
templates.businessImpact: Single-circuit internet failure stops cloud apps, payments, VoIP, and remote work for many SMBs. Without a resilience plan, outages become all-or-nothing events with no agreed temporary path.

templates.title: Maintain DNS, DHCP, and other core network services
templates.description:
Finding: DNS, DHCP, and related core services are not consistently maintained. “No” typically means unmanaged or unknown ownership of these services; “Partially” usually means they work day-to-day without backups, documentation, or clear change control.

Recommended action: Identify where DNS and DHCP (and any other critical name/address services in scope) run today. Place them on supported infrastructure with configuration backups, define who may change scopes and records, and document recovery steps if the service host fails. Eliminate temporary or desktop-hosted core services on business networks.

Expected outcome: Address and name resolution remain available and recoverable, reducing unexplained “network is down” incidents that are actually core-service failures.

Implementation considerations: Coordinate changes carefully—DHCP/DNS mistakes can outage an entire site. Keep reverse/forward DNS aligned for key servers. Pair with monitoring (NW-008) so service failures alert before users flood the help desk.
templates.businessImpact: When DNS, DHCP, or related core services are unstable or undocumented, users lose connectivity even when circuits and firewalls are healthy. Informal “someone’s PC is the DHCP server” patterns create fragile single points of failure.

templates.title: Monitor the network for availability and performance issues
templates.description:
Finding: Proactive network monitoring is missing or limited. “No” typically means no availability or performance monitoring for critical network paths; “Partially” usually means some devices are watched while circuits, wireless controllers, or remote sites are not.

Recommended action: Monitor critical network devices and internet/edge availability with alerting to an accountable responder. Include basic signals such as device down, high utilization, or circuit loss for in-scope sites. Review recurring alerts and close noisy or orphaned monitors.

Expected outcome: Network problems are noticed earlier, shortening outages and reducing reliance on user reports as the primary detection method.

Implementation considerations: Start with a small set of high-value monitors to avoid alert fatigue. This recommendation focuses on network health/availability—not full security-event detection covered under Security Operations. Align after-hours expectations with business risk.
templates.businessImpact: Without proactive network monitoring, outages and degraded circuits are discovered only when users complain. Late detection extends downtime and makes root-cause analysis harder after the fact.

templates.title: Maintain physical network infrastructure in workable condition
templates.description:
Finding: Physical network infrastructure maintenance is missing or inconsistent. “No” typically means closets, cabling, or power for network gear are neglected; “Partially” usually means some sites are orderly while others have unlabeled patching, UPS gaps, or environmental issues.

Recommended action: Inspect primary network closets and racks for safe power, reasonable airflow, labeled patching, and clear access. Remediate damaged cabling and unsupported mounting. Establish a light periodic check (for example quarterly) for critical sites and after moves or renovations.

Expected outcome: Physical faults and accidental outages decline, and support staff can work in closets without guesswork.

Implementation considerations: Keep scope proportional—focus on rooms that house edge and core gear. Coordinate electrical or HVAC work with facilities. Low priority relative to firewall and segmentation gaps, but often cheap to improve.
templates.businessImpact: Neglected cabling, power, cooling, or closet organization causes intermittent faults that are expensive to diagnose. Physical neglect also raises accidental disconnect and environmental failure risk.

templates.title: Keep network documentation current after changes
templates.description:
Finding: Network documentation is not kept current. “No” typically means usable network docs are absent or abandoned; “Partially” usually means initial diagrams exist but are outdated after moves, circuit changes, or equipment swaps.

Recommended action: Maintain a practical network package (sites, circuits, edge devices, major VLANs/zones, and critical paths) and update it after material changes. Assign who updates the package and where the current version is stored. Spot-check currency during planned maintenance windows.

Expected outcome: Support staff and providers can orient quickly during outages and changes without reconstructing the network from memory.

Implementation considerations: Complements Documentation & Knowledge network documentation recommendations by focusing on currency after change, not the first-time creation of a full documentation program. Prefer simple living diagrams over elaborate unused tools. Protect docs that reveal addressing or credentials.
templates.businessImpact: Stale network diagrams and inventories slow incident response and make vendor handoffs unreliable. Documentation that exists but is never updated after changes recreates tribal-knowledge risk.

templates.title: Include all critical systems in backups
templates.description:
Finding: Not all critical systems are included in backups, or coverage is incomplete. “No” typically means backup scope is unclear or major systems are unprotected; “Partially” usually means some servers or SaaS workloads are backed up while others—often newer systems, cloud apps, or shared drives—are not.

Recommended action: List systems and data stores that the business cannot afford to lose (servers, file shares, email/cloud collaboration, line-of-business apps, and databases in scope). Confirm each has a backup job or equivalent protected copy, close gaps, and record what is intentionally excluded with a business owner. Revisit coverage when systems are added.

Expected outcome: Recovery options exist for the systems that matter most, reducing the chance that an outage becomes irreversible data loss.

Implementation considerations: Include SaaS and cloud workloads, not only on-premises servers. Pair with critical-data identification (DP-008) so scope is business-driven. Validate job success separately from “a backup product is installed.”
templates.businessImpact: Critical systems left out of backups turn routine failures, ransomware, or accidental deletion into prolonged outages or permanent data loss. Incomplete coverage is one of the most common and costly recovery failures for SMBs.

templates.title: Monitor backup jobs for success and failure
templates.description:
Finding: Backup monitoring is missing or inconsistent. “No” suggests nobody regularly reviews job outcomes; “Partially” suggests some jobs are watched while others fail silently or alerts go unowned.

Recommended action: Enable failure and missed-job alerting for backup workloads that protect critical systems. Assign who reviews alerts on business days, define escalation for repeated failures, and keep a simple record of unresolved backup issues until closed.

Expected outcome: Backup problems are noticed while they are still fixable, instead of during an emergency restore.

Implementation considerations: Tune alerts to avoid noise from known maintenance windows. Monitoring without ownership does not help—name a responder. Separate “job reported success” from restore-test validation (DP-003).
templates.businessImpact: Unmonitored backups create false confidence—failures can accumulate unnoticed until restore is needed. Detecting failed or incomplete jobs early preserves the recovery window.

templates.title: Perform restore tests on a regular schedule
templates.description:
Finding: Restore tests are not performed regularly. “No” typically means restores are only attempted during real emergencies; “Partially” usually means occasional ad hoc tests without a schedule, scope, or recorded results.

Recommended action: Establish a recurring restore-test cadence for representative critical workloads (for example quarterly for highest-value systems, with spot checks after major backup changes). Record what was restored, how long it took, and what failed. Remediate gaps discovered in testing.

Expected outcome: Leadership gains evidence that backups can actually recover needed data within a useful timeframe.

Implementation considerations: Test restores into isolated targets to avoid overwriting production. Start with the systems that would stop the business first. Document lessons without treating every test as a full disaster rehearsal unless planned.
templates.businessImpact: Backups that are never restore-tested may be incomplete, unrestorable, or too slow for business needs. Regular tests are how organizations learn whether recovery will work before a real incident.

templates.title: Maintain a practical disaster recovery plan
templates.description:
Finding: A disaster recovery plan is missing or incomplete. “No” suggests no documented technical recovery approach; “Partially” suggests notes or vendor runbooks exist but are outdated, untested, or unknown to the people who would use them.

Recommended action: Create a concise DR plan covering critical systems, backup/recovery sources, restoration sequence, roles, and communication during a major outage or data-loss event. Store it where responders can reach it offline if primary systems are unavailable. Review after material infrastructure changes and after restore tests.

Expected outcome: Responders follow a known sequence instead of inventing recovery order during a crisis, improving speed and coordination.

Implementation considerations: Prefer a living runbook over a lengthy unread binder. Align technical recovery steps with business continuity priorities (DP-005) and recovery objectives (DP-006). Include provider contacts and break-glass access paths.
templates.businessImpact: Without a disaster recovery plan, teams improvise under pressure, extending downtime and increasing the chance of conflicting decisions. A usable plan shortens the path from incident to restored systems.

templates.title: Maintain a business continuity plan for critical operations
templates.description:
Finding: A business continuity plan is missing or only partially defined. “No” typically means no agreed approach for operating through major disruption; “Partially” usually means informal workarounds exist without documented priorities, roles, or triggers.

Recommended action: Identify critical business functions and how they continue during prolonged IT outages (manual processes, alternate sites or remote work, key vendor contacts, and decision authority). Document activation criteria, communication expectations, and handoffs to technical recovery. Review with leadership at a defined cadence.

Expected outcome: The organization can sustain essential operations while technology is restored, rather than freezing until every system returns.

Implementation considerations: Keep the plan proportional to business size—prioritize a few critical functions first. Distinguish BCP (business operations) from DR (technology restore) clearly so owners do not assume one document covers both. Involve operations leaders, not only IT.
templates.businessImpact: Technology recovery alone does not keep the business running if people lack alternate ways to serve customers, process payroll, or communicate. Continuity planning reduces revenue and reputation damage while systems are restored.

templates.title: Define recovery time and recovery point objectives
templates.description:
Finding: Recovery objectives are not defined or are only informal. “No” suggests no RTO/RPO-style targets exist; “Partially” suggests some targets are discussed for a few systems without documented agreement or alignment to backup design.

Recommended action: For each critical system or data class, define target recovery time (how quickly it must return) and recovery point (how much data loss is tolerable). Use those targets to validate backup frequency, retention, and restore-test expectations. Review when business priorities change.

Expected outcome: Backup and DR investments match business tolerance for downtime and data loss, making recovery design measurable.

Implementation considerations: Use plain language with leaders (“email back same day,” “lose at most one hour of entries”) before introducing acronyms. Objectives should be ambitious but achievable—aspirational targets without funding create false confidence. Feed results into DR planning and backup scope decisions.
templates.businessImpact: Without agreed recovery objectives, backup design and vendor expectations drift from what the business actually needs. Ambiguous targets lead to underinvestment in critical systems and overinvestment in low-impact ones.

templates.title: Protect backups from compromise and tampering
templates.description:
Finding: Backups are not adequately protected from compromise. “No” typically means backup stores are reachable with the same privileged access as production; “Partially” usually means some immutability, offline, or separate-credential controls exist without consistent coverage.

Recommended action: Separate backup administrative credentials from ordinary production administrative access so routine domain or server admins cannot delete, alter retention, or encrypt backup repositories by default. Enable immutability, offline, or air-gapped copies for critical backup sets according to platform capability, restrict who can change backup jobs, and monitor backup infrastructure for suspicious changes. Confirm at least one recovery copy would survive a production-wide credential compromise scenario appropriate to business risk.

Expected outcome: A recoverable copy is more likely to remain intact when production systems are attacked or mistakenly wiped.

Implementation considerations: Perfect isolation is not always feasible—prioritize critical backup repositories first. Coordinate with identity and privileged-access practices so backup admin accounts are few, monitored, and distinct from day-to-day production admin roles. Test that protected copies can still be restored by authorized responders.
templates.businessImpact: Backups that share the same access path as production can be encrypted or deleted by the same incident that destroys primary data. Hardening backup copies preserves a clean recovery path after ransomware or insider misuse.

templates.title: Identify critical data for protection and recovery priority
templates.description:
Finding: Critical data has not been clearly identified, or identification is incomplete. “No” suggests no agreed data priorities; “Partially” suggests some systems are labeled critical without a shared inventory of data classes and owners.

Recommended action: Work with business leaders to list critical data classes (for example financial records, customer files, operational databases, and email/collaboration content in scope). Map each to systems, owners, and recovery priority. Use the list to drive backup inclusion, retention, and restore-test selection.

Expected outcome: Protection and recovery effort concentrates on data the business cannot afford to lose or rebuild slowly.

Implementation considerations: Keep the first version short and executive-readable. Update when major applications change. Complements backup coverage (DP-001) by defining what matters before how it is copied.
templates.businessImpact: Without knowing which data is critical, backup scope and restore order become guesswork. Teams may protect low-value stores thoroughly while under-protecting the records that actually run the business.

templates.title: Document data retention requirements
templates.description:
Finding: Retention requirements are not documented or are only partially defined. “No” typically means no written retention guidance; “Partially” usually means some systems have settings while business and legal expectations remain unclear.

Recommended action: Document retention expectations for major data classes (how long backups and primary records should be kept, and any legal or contractual drivers known to the business). Align backup retention settings to those expectations where practical, and record intentional differences. Review when regulations or contracts change.

Expected outcome: Retention becomes an intentional business decision rather than an accident of default backup settings.

Implementation considerations: This recommendation does not replace formal legal counsel—capture known requirements and escalate uncertain obligations. Avoid promising compliance certification. Start with the few data classes that drive the most risk.
templates.businessImpact: Undocumented retention leads to keeping everything forever—or deleting too soon. Either outcome creates legal, operational, or storage risk and complicates restore and e-discovery expectations.

templates.title: Assign ownership for recovery readiness
templates.description:
Finding: Recovery ownership is missing or unclear. “No” suggests no accountable owner for backups, restore testing, and DR readiness; “Partially” suggests fragmented responsibility across vendors and staff without a single accountable lead.

Recommended action: Assign a primary owner accountable for backup coverage, monitoring follow-up, restore-test cadence, and DR plan currency. Define how that owner escalates to business leadership when recovery objectives cannot be met. Communicate the owner to providers and executives who would declare a disaster.

Expected outcome: Recovery gaps have a durable owner, so issues found in monitoring or tests are closed rather than rediscovered after the next incident.

Implementation considerations: Ownership may combine a technical provider lead with an internal business sponsor. Authority to prioritize restore tests and budget matters as much as tool expertise. Align with overall technology leadership so recovery is not treated as “the backup vendor’s problem alone.”
templates.businessImpact: Backup products without a recovery owner still fail in practice—failed jobs, stale plans, and untested restores go unaddressed. Clear ownership keeps recovery readiness current between assessments.

templates.title: Standardize centrally administered productivity capabilities
templates.description:
Finding: Standardized, centrally administered productivity capabilities are missing or only partially adopted. “No” typically means core collaboration still relies on personal accounts or disconnected tools; “Partially” usually means administered capabilities exist but material teams remain outside them. Organizations do not need a single vendor or suite for every business function—the gap is lack of consistent administration for core productivity work.

Recommended action: Establish or complete centrally administered capabilities for email, calendar, and core file collaboration for in-scope staff. Migrate remaining holdouts with a cutover plan, and retire personal-account use for business communication where policy requires. Confirm identity join/leave processes cover those capabilities. Specialty or departmental tools may remain where they serve distinct needs, provided core productivity work is administered consistently.

Expected outcome: Employees work in administered environments that are supportable and controllable, improving offboarding reliability and making security and retention settings practical for core collaboration.

Implementation considerations: Plan migration waves by department. Confirm licensing and mailbox/file size needs before forced cutover. Coordinate with Identity & Access for sign-in standards. Remain vendor-agnostic—focus on central administration and ownership rather than mandating one product for all functions.
templates.businessImpact: When email, calendar, and core file collaboration are scattered across personal accounts or disconnected tools, support and offboarding become inconsistent and security controls are hard to apply evenly. Standardized, centrally administered productivity capabilities give the organization a manageable baseline for day-to-day work.

templates.title: Enable secure employee access to required business files
templates.description:
Finding: Secure access to required files is incomplete. “No” typically means no dependable shared file approach for core roles; “Partially” usually means some teams have structured access while others rely on insecure workarounds.

Recommended action: Provide a standard, permissioned way for employees to reach the business files they need (cloud file platform and/or secured file shares in scope). Define access by role, enable secure remote access paths, and reduce reliance on emailed attachments for living documents. Review permissions when people change roles.

Expected outcome: Staff find and update authoritative files without unsafe sharing shortcuts, improving both productivity and control.

Implementation considerations: Start with the highest-friction teams (remote workers, multi-site groups). Align permissions with least privilege. Complements Data Protection backup scope once file locations are known. Avoid promising a full records-management program in the first pass.
templates.businessImpact: When staff cannot reliably and securely reach the files they need, work shifts to email attachments, USB drives, and unsanctioned sharing. That slows execution and increases data-leak and version-chaos risk.

templates.title: Standardize how business documents are organized
templates.description:
Finding: Document organization is not standardized. “No” typically means no agreed structure for shared business files; “Partially” usually means some departments follow conventions while others do not.

Recommended action: Define a simple organization standard for shared workspaces (top-level structure, naming conventions, and ownership of key libraries). Migrate or map high-value content into that structure, and publish brief guidance for staff. Assign library owners who keep structures from re-fragmenting.

Expected outcome: Employees spend less time hunting for files, and shared content remains navigable as the organization grows.

Implementation considerations: Keep the standard lightweight—overdesigned taxonomies fail. Do not boil the ocean; prioritize active business libraries first. Pair with PC-002 so organization work lands in the approved access platform.
templates.businessImpact: Ad hoc folder sprawl and inconsistent naming waste time and cause version errors. Standardization reduces search friction and makes onboarding and audits far simpler.

templates.title: Standardize collaboration tools for teams
templates.description:
Finding: Collaboration tools are not standardized. “No” typically means teams pick tools independently; “Partially” usually means a preferred stack exists but unsanctioned alternatives remain common for day-to-day work.

Recommended action: Designate approved collaboration tools for messaging, meetings, and team workspaces. Communicate the standard, migrate high-traffic teams, and retire redundant tools where practical. Define how exceptions are requested and reviewed.

Expected outcome: Teams collaborate in fewer, supported channels, improving findability of decisions and reducing shadow-IT sprawl.

Implementation considerations: Choose tools that integrate with the productivity platform where possible. Address cultural adoption—mandate without enablement fails. Distinct from PC-001 (core productivity capabilities) by focusing on team collaboration channels and meeting norms.
templates.businessImpact: Multiple chat, meeting, and whiteboard tools fragment conversations and complicate security and retention. Standardization reduces tool sprawl and makes support and training feasible.

templates.title: Support secure mobile and on-the-go work
templates.description:
Finding: Secure mobile work is not adequately supported. “No” typically means no approved way to work from phones/tablets; “Partially” usually means some apps work while others force insecure workarounds.

Recommended action: Define which business functions must work on mobile (email, files, line-of-business apps in scope) and enable them through approved apps or secure browser access. Set expectations for device PIN/biometrics and lost-device reporting. Limit download of sensitive files to unmanaged personal devices where policy requires.

Expected outcome: Mobile and traveling staff can complete essential work through supported channels instead of unsafe improvisation.

Implementation considerations: Complements Endpoint encryption recommendations by focusing on how work is done on mobile, not solely full-disk encryption of company laptops. Clarify BYOD vs company-owned device rules. Start with the roles that travel most.
templates.businessImpact: Mobile work without a supported pattern pushes staff toward personal email, unsecured apps, and local copies of business data. A clear secure-mobile approach protects productivity for field and traveling roles.

templates.title: Standardize core business applications
templates.description:
Finding: Business applications are not standardized. “No” typically means teams adopt tools independently for the same job; “Partially” usually means preferred applications exist without consistent enforcement or retirement of duplicates.

Recommended action: Inventory applications used for major business functions, designate preferred standards where duplication exists, and plan consolidation or controlled exceptions. Publish an approved application list for common roles and review additions through a lightweight intake process.

Expected outcome: Support, training, and security effort concentrate on a manageable application set rather than an ever-growing shadow portfolio.

Implementation considerations: Distinct from Technology Strategy application review cadence (strategy/governance)—this recommendation focuses on operational standardization for day-to-day productivity. Involve department owners so standards are usable. Do not force specialty tools into a one-size-fits-all suite.
templates.businessImpact: Uncontrolled application variety increases license cost, training burden, and integration failures. Standardization improves supportability and makes security reviews practical.

templates.title: Manage software licenses intentionally
templates.description:
Finding: Software license management is missing or incomplete. “No” typically means no clear inventory of entitlements and assignments; “Partially” usually means some major suites are tracked while others are purchased ad hoc.

Recommended action: Maintain a living view of major software entitlements, assigned users, and renewal dates for productivity and line-of-business tools in scope. Reclaim unused seats during offboarding and before renewals. Align purchases to the approved application standards where practical.

Expected outcome: License spend better matches real usage, and renewal surprises decline.

Implementation considerations: Complements Documentation & Knowledge licensing/warranty recordkeeping by focusing on active assignment and renewal management for software seats. Start with the highest-cost suites. Avoid legal certification claims—capture known entitlements and escalate unclear obligations.
templates.businessImpact: Unmanaged licenses cause overspending, surprise true-ups, and compliance exposure—or leave staff without seats they need. Intentional license management ties spend to actual use.

templates.title: Reduce high-friction manual workflows with technology
templates.description:
Finding: Manual workflows have not been systematically improved with technology. “No” typically means known paper/email-heavy processes remain untouched; “Partially” usually means a few automations exist without a prioritized pipeline of improvements.

Recommended action: Identify a short list of high-friction manual processes (for example intake, approvals, status tracking, or handoffs). Select one or two to improve using existing productivity/collaboration capabilities or lightweight workflow tools. Measure whether handoff time or error rates improve, then iterate.

Expected outcome: Staff reclaim time from repetitive work, and process quality becomes less dependent on heroic manual effort.

Implementation considerations: Prefer improving processes the business already owns over buying new platforms first. Avoid automation theater—pick workflows with clear owners and measurable pain. Do not promise enterprise-wide transformation in a single engagement.
templates.businessImpact: Manual, repetitive workflows consume staff time and introduce errors that technology can often reduce. Leaving known friction unaddressed caps productivity gains from platforms the organization already owns.

templates.title: Ensure employees have the technology needed to succeed
templates.description:
Finding: Employees do not consistently have the technology needed to succeed. “No” typically means material role gaps in devices or required tools; “Partially” usually means some teams are well equipped while others operate with chronic deficits.

Recommended action: Define role-based technology baselines (device class, core apps, and peripherals) for major job families. Survey or sample gaps against that baseline, and remediate the highest-impact shortages first. Revisit baselines when roles or software standards change.

Expected outcome: Staff can perform expected work without fighting inadequate tools, improving throughput and reducing shadow purchases.

Implementation considerations: Coordinate with Endpoint lifecycle and Technology Strategy refresh planning for hardware. Keep baselines realistic for SMB budgets. Capture exceptions intentionally rather than letting gaps linger silently.
templates.businessImpact: Underpowered devices, missing peripherals, or lack of required software create quiet productivity losses and workarounds. Equipping roles appropriately is foundational to every other productivity investment.

templates.title: Assign ownership for productivity and collaboration improvements
templates.description:
Finding: Responsibility for productivity improvements is missing or unclear. “No” suggests no accountable owner; “Partially” suggests informal interest without authority, cadence, or coverage across departments.

Recommended action: Assign a primary owner (internal lead and/or provider counterpart) accountable for productivity platform standards, collaboration tool governance, and the improvement backlog for high-friction workflows. Define a simple review cadence with business stakeholders. Communicate the owner to department managers who request new tools.

Expected outcome: Productivity gaps have a durable owner, so standards and improvements persist between assessment cycles.

Implementation considerations: Ownership can combine an operations or office lead with IT/provider support. Authority to set standards matters more than deep technical skill. Align with overall technology leadership so tool decisions are not orphaned.
templates.businessImpact: Without a named owner, platform sprawl, license waste, and workflow friction recur after one-time cleanups. Durable ownership keeps productivity standards current as teams and tools change.

templates.title: Implement monitoring for security-relevant system events
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate systems are not adequately monitored for security events. This reflects reported capability, not confirmation that a specific incident was missed.

Recommended action: Define high-value log sources (identity sign-ins, email security, endpoints, firewalls, servers, backups). Enable alerting for suspicious sign-in, malware detections, and privileged changes. Ensure someone is accountable for triage during business hours and for after-hours escalation paths appropriate to business risk.

Expected outcome: Suspicious activity is more likely to be noticed while containment is still feasible, reducing the duration and impact of security events.

Implementation considerations: Start with a focused alert set to avoid noise. Confirm log retention and timezone consistency. If a managed detection service is used, clarify which alerts remain the customer's responsibility.
templates.businessImpact: Without monitoring, unauthorized access, malware activity, or failed attack attempts may go unnoticed until downtime or data loss is already underway. Late detection typically increases recovery time and cost for an SMB.

templates.title: Assess and remediate vulnerabilities on a regular schedule
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate vulnerabilities are not assessed regularly. This is an assessment maturity finding and does not by itself prove a specific exploitable flaw is present.

Recommended action: Establish recurring external and/or internal vulnerability scanning for in-scope systems, prioritize remediations by severity and business criticality, and track closure. Include cloud and remote-access assets. Schedule authenticated scans where credentials improve accuracy.

Expected outcome: Known weaknesses are identified and reduced systematically, lowering the likelihood that publicly known exploits disrupt operations.

Implementation considerations: Coordinate scan windows to avoid performance impact on line-of-business systems. Maintain an exception process for risk-accepted findings with owners and review dates. Align remediation with change management.
templates.businessImpact: Unpatched or misconfigured systems can expose organizations to preventable security incidents and operational disruptions. Without recurring vulnerability assessment, known weaknesses can accumulate across servers, endpoints, and Internet-facing services.

templates.title: Apply security updates promptly across critical systems
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate security updates may not be applied promptly. This finding is based on reported practices rather than a verified patch-compliance inventory.

Recommended action: Define patch SLAs by system class (for example, critical Internet-facing and privileged systems first). Use centralized update tooling where available, test high-risk updates when practical, and report compliance to ownership. Include firmware and third-party apps in scope for high-value assets.

Expected outcome: Exposure windows shrink for known vulnerabilities, and update practices become predictable rather than reactive.

Implementation considerations: Balance speed with change risk—emergency patches for actively exploited issues may bypass normal delays. Maintain rollback plans for core systems. Coordinate with application owners who restrict update timing.
templates.businessImpact: Delayed patching leaves known defects available to attackers and can also cause instability when updates pile up. For SMBs, a single unpatched Internet-facing or backup-related system can drive outsized downtime and recovery expense.

templates.title: Deliver recurring security awareness training for employees
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate employees do not consistently receive security awareness training. This is a process finding from the assessment, not evidence of a particular user failure.

Recommended action: Implement a recurring training program covering phishing, credential protection, data handling, and reporting channels. Include new-hire onboarding and at least annual refreshers. Consider periodic simulated phishing only if results are used for coaching rather than punishment.

Expected outcome: Staff are more likely to pause on suspicious messages and report issues early, improving the organization's human layer of defense.

Implementation considerations: Keep modules short and role-relevant. Ensure reporting of suspicious email is easy. Coordinate with leadership so training completion is an expected business habit, not an IT-only initiative.
templates.businessImpact: Many incidents begin with phishing, unsafe downloads, or accidental data sharing. Without regular awareness training, staff are less prepared to recognize social engineering, which increases the likelihood of account compromise and business email fraud.

templates.title: Establish a practical incident response process
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate an incident response process is missing or incomplete. This reflects preparedness maturity from the assessment, not that an incident is currently active.

Recommended action: Document a concise response plan: severity definitions, internal contacts, provider escalation, containment steps for common scenarios (malware, mailbox compromise, lost device), evidence preservation basics, and communication guidelines. Run a brief tabletop exercise annually and update contacts after org changes.

Expected outcome: The organization can respond faster and more consistently under pressure, limiting operational disruption and supporting clearer decision-making.

Implementation considerations: Keep the plan usable under stress—checklists beat long manuals. Store contacts where they are reachable if email is unavailable. Align with cyber-insurance or legal notification expectations if those already apply to the business.
templates.businessImpact: When an incident occurs without a defined response process, teams lose time deciding who to call, what to isolate, and how to communicate. That delay increases downtime, data-loss risk, and confusion for customers and staff.

templates.title: Retain security logs long enough to support investigations
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate security logs may not be retained adequately. This is based on assessment responses, not a forensic review of current log stores.

Recommended action: Identify critical log sources and set retention appropriate to business and investigative needs (commonly weeks to months for SMB security-relevant logs, longer for high-value systems where feasible). Protect logs from tampering, confirm time sync, and ensure responsible parties know how to retrieve them.

Expected outcome: Investigations and post-incident reviews have usable history, improving root-cause analysis and confidence in containment.

Implementation considerations: Balance retention cost with value—prioritize identity, email, endpoint, and firewall logs first. Confirm privacy and contractual constraints. If logs are held by a provider, document how the customer requests exports.
templates.businessImpact: Short or inconsistent log retention makes it difficult to determine how an incident started, what was accessed, and whether the issue is fully contained. That uncertainty prolongs recovery and weakens accountability with customers or partners when questions arise.

templates.title: Review technology and security risks on a recurring cadence
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate technology risks are not reviewed periodically in a structured way. This is a governance finding from the assessment.

Recommended action: Schedule a recurring risk review (for example quarterly) covering open security recommendations, major system changes, backup readiness, vendor access, and incidents or near-misses. Capture owners and next actions in a simple register reviewed by business leadership and IT support.

Expected outcome: Risk decisions become intentional, overdue items surface earlier, and technology investment aligns more closely with business exposure.

Implementation considerations: Keep the register short enough to maintain. Tie reviews to existing leadership meetings where possible. Avoid creating a parallel bureaucracy that will not be sustained.
templates.businessImpact: Without periodic risk review, known issues linger, new tools introduce unmanaged exposure, and leadership lacks a clear picture of technology risk relative to business priorities. That leads to reactive spending and surprise outages or incidents.

templates.title: Include third-party and vendor access in security risk decisions
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate third-party risk may not be considered consistently. This is an assessment-reported governance gap, not an allegation against a specific vendor.

Recommended action: Inventory vendors with access to systems or sensitive data. For material providers, review access paths, require MFA where applicable, remove dormant accounts, and capture basic security expectations in onboarding/offboarding. Revisit access when contracts change.

Expected outcome: External access becomes intentional and reviewable, reducing lingering vendor privileges and clarifying responsibilities when a provider incident occurs.

Implementation considerations: Proportionate effort matters—deep questionnaires are unnecessary for every small tool. Focus on vendors with privileged access, financial data, or production system reach.
templates.businessImpact: Vendors and SaaS platforms often hold sensitive data or privileged remote access. If third-party risk is ignored, a provider weakness or leftover vendor account can disrupt operations or expose information outside the company's direct control.

templates.title: Assign clear ownership for security operations responsibilities
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate security ownership may not be clearly assigned. This is an organizational finding from the assessment.

Recommended action: Designate a business-side owner for security outcomes and document which tasks are performed internally versus by an IT provider. Clarify who approves exceptions, who is contacted during incidents, and how recommendations are prioritized. Review the RACI when providers change.

Expected outcome: Accountability is explicit, reducing dropped tasks and speeding decisions when security issues arise.

Implementation considerations: Ownership does not require a full-time CISO for most SMBs; a named manager plus provider support is often enough if responsibilities are written down.
templates.businessImpact: Unclear security ownership leads to missed alerts, delayed patching decisions, and confusion during incidents. Leadership may assume "IT handles it" while providers assume the customer owns risk acceptance—leaving gaps that only appear under pressure.

templates.title: Continuously improve security practices based on incidents and reviews
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate security practices are not continuously improved in a deliberate way. This reflects reported maturity, not a grade on any single control.

Recommended action: After incidents, near-misses, audits, or quarterly reviews, capture a small set of improvement actions with owners and due dates. Revisit policies, alerting, and training content when recurring issues appear. Track completion in the same register used for technology risk review.

Expected outcome: Security effort stays aligned to real weaknesses over time rather than one-time projects that slowly decay.

Implementation considerations: Limit work-in-progress—few completed improvements beat a long unfinished list. Review closed actions in leadership meetings to sustain the habit.
